label: Title
notes: Open by placing the lecture inside the manifest row and the chapter span. The subject is not just detecting one intersection; it is building a disciplined sweep that can report every crossing among closed segments while preparing the data structures needed later for map overlay.

label: Overlay Motivation
notes: Use the synthetic map to make the application concrete. Roads, rivers, and regions each carry partial information, but overlaying them creates new vertices and faces that answer richer questions. The chapter's algorithms are motivated by this need to turn layered geometry into searchable combinatorial structure.

label: Closed Segments
notes: Emphasize that the input objects are closed line segments, so endpoints are part of the segment and can be genuine intersections. This is why the predicate must distinguish proper interior crossings from endpoint contacts; otherwise the sweep will miss events or count them inconsistently.

label: Output Sensitivity
notes: The brute force grid is easy to trust because it tests every pair, but it spends time on pairs that are far apart and never interact. The sparse drawing shows why the target complexity should depend on the number of reported intersections as well as the number of input segments.

label: Failed Interval Sweep
notes: Walk through the tempting one-dimensional idea: sweep by x and keep segments whose x-intervals overlap the sweep position. The vertical probe makes the failure visible, because many active segments can share an x-range while being far apart in y, producing too many candidate tests.

label: Sweep State
notes: Introduce the two pieces of state slowly. The event queue orders points lexicographically from top to bottom, and the active tree stores the vertical order of segments cut by the sweep line. The entire algorithm is a conversation between these two ordered structures.

label: Local Adjacency
notes: The local adjacency rule is the central economy of the sweep. If two segments are separated in the active order by another segment at the current sweep position, they cannot be the next pair to meet below that position. Only neighbors need to be scheduled for future tests.

label: Lemma 2.1
notes: Present this as a visual proof rather than a formal detour. Just above an interior crossing, the two crossing segments have no other segment between them in sweep order; otherwise that intervening segment would have to pass through the tiny lens around the crossing point.

label: Event Cases
notes: Explain the three sets attached to an event point. U contains segments starting at the point, L contains segments ending there, and C contains segments passing through from above to below. Clustered events matter because several segments may meet at the same coordinates.

label: Algorithm Dashboard
notes: Use the dashboard as a rehearsal of the whole sweep. Pop the next event, report the intersection when multiple incident segments meet, update the active order, and then test the new adjacent pairs. The visual separates queue, status tree, and output list so the invariants stay visible.

label: Correctness Invariant
notes: The correctness invariant says that everything strictly above the sweep line has already been handled. Events are processed in priority order, and every future crossing must first become a neighbor crossing that gets inserted into the queue. This turns local tests into global completeness.

label: Runtime Count
notes: Connect the running time to counting events. There are two endpoints per segment and one event for each discovered intersection point. Splitting the arrangement into a planar graph supplies the geometric intuition that the output size bounds the extra work caused by crossings.

label: DCEL Records
notes: Shift from detecting intersections to representing the subdivided map. The DCEL stores vertices, faces, and directed half-edges with explicit twin, next, previous, origin, and incident-face pointers. The benefit is local navigation around boundaries after the overlay creates many small pieces.

label: Overlay Splits
notes: The overlay step is a controlled surgery on the DCEL. When an edge passes through a vertex or two edges cross, the affected half-edges are split and rewired so that the next and previous pointers still trace valid boundary cycles in the refined subdivision.

label: Face Recovery
notes: After all splits, faces are recovered by walking boundary cycles. Labels are inherited from the two input subdivisions, so each output face knows which face of S1 and which face of S2 contains it. Holes require special attention because not every boundary cycle is an outer boundary.

label: Boolean Operations
notes: Close by translating labels into operations. Union, intersection, and difference do not require a new geometric algorithm once the overlay is built; they select faces by truth conditions on membership in the two inputs. Mention that the chapter excludes overlapping segment interiors and that more optimal variants exist.
